Days ago, OpenAI accused Apple of improperly introducing new evidence in a trade secrets case. Today, Apple is firing back, alleging that OpenAI exceeded the limits permitted by court rules in its response. Details below.

Apple argues that OpenAI has done more than merely oppose the new evidence — it has gone a step further.

In Apple's lawsuit against two former employees (Chang Liu and Tang Tan), OpenAI, and io Products over alleged trade secret theft, one of the points of contention involves Apple's request for a temporary restraining order (TRO).

In a nutshell, Apple is asking the court to issue a TRO on the grounds that doing so will prevent its trade secrets from being further embedded into OpenAI's hardware development while the case is ongoing.

In the legal filings exchanged between the two sides, Apple submitted a response brief along with five expert declarations. The defendants subsequently accused Apple of improperly introducing new evidence and asked the court to strike portions of the filings.

In their opposition brief, OpenAI and the other defendants went beyond merely claiming that Apple had introduced new evidence — they submitted additional filings to counter Apple's arguments.

Apple filed its response to those opposition briefs today, accusing the defendants of doing more than simply opposing the new evidence and instead raising a fresh set of arguments and evidentiary submissions:

Under Local Rule 7-3(d)(1), a party may oppose new evidence in a response brief, but the rule also provides that the filing "must not contain further argument in support of the motion." The defendants did not comply with that limitation, and instead used their filing to re-litigate the substance of Apple's TRO motion. For instance, the defendants question whether Dr. Runge "has any basis to perform any analysis," whether he has adequately addressed "contradictory evidence," and whether he can establish that certain Apple materials are not publicly available. […] These arguments are not oppositions to new evidence. (Arguments that "certain portions of the plaintiff's argument are unsupported by evidence or contradicted by other testimony" are not "oppositions to evidence.")

Apple also objected to a new declaration submitted by Liu, describing it as the defendants' "most egregious overreach":

Notably, when submitting Liu's declaration, the defendants stated that the declaration should only be considered if the court simultaneously decided to consider the Apple evidence the defendants had challenged.

Apple argued that, since the defendants have now raised a fresh set of arguments of their own, the court should consider the full record rather than strike any of the evidence from Apple's response brief:

The court is scheduled to hear Apple's request for a TRO on October 14.
